docs.bounded.component: `Bounded` gives a node a box: the area it occupies on the desk.
One shape answers three questions — what a finger can hit, what a shadow is cast from, and
how much room the owner's layout has to leave for it — so it is one atom rather than three
fields that could drift apart.
```ts
import { node, Bounded, footprint, rect, star } from "game-kit"
const card = node("card", Bounded({ bounds: rect(1, 1.4) }))
const badge = node("badge", Bounded({ bounds: star(5, 1, 0.42) }))
footprint(node("ghost"))   // undefined — a node without Bounded has no box
## One field, and one kind of value
The field is `bounds`, and its value is a `Shape`: a start point and a list of segments, each
one a straight run or a cubic curve. That is all a shape is. There are no sorts.
```ts
interface Shape {
start: Point
segments: { to: Point; c1?: Point; c2?: Point }[]
There used to be four — `rect`, `circle`, `poly`, `path` — and every consumer branched on the
tag: flattening, extent, transform, the contour walk. Four branches for a distinction the
geometry does not have. A rect IS a path of four straight runs. A circle IS an ellipse with
equal radii — not a scaled anything, and not a sort. A polygon IS a path with no curves.
## The shapes you actually write
Nobody writes a card as four segments, so what a designer reaches for are HELPERS — ordinary
functions the kit exports, each returning a path:
```ts
rect(w, h)                 roundedRect(w, h, radius)
circle(r)                  ellipse(rx, ry)
polygon(corners, r)        star(points, outer, inner)
polyline(points)           fromSvgPath(d)
A new shape is a new function, and nothing downstream changes: a star is not a case the
renderer has to learn, it is a path that flattens like every other. It also reads: `star(5, 1,
0.42)` says what it is where twenty coordinates say nothing.
`fromSvgPath` takes the `d` out of Figma, Illustrator or an `.svg` file — straight runs,
cubics, quadratics and the shorthands, absolute or relative. `A`, the elliptical arc, is the
one command not handled, and it returns nothing rather than quietly dropping a piece.
## The origin
`(0,0)` in a shape's own coordinates is the point everything is measured from: `at` puts THAT
somewhere, and a rotation will turn about THAT. There is no `pivot` field and there is not
going to be one — a different origin is a different node, and composition already says that.
Every helper here builds its shape around zero. A path you paste carries whatever coordinates
its author wrote, so it may sit far off its own origin. Switch on `bounds` in the toolbar and
the cross in the middle is exactly this point; switch on `grid` and you can read the size off
the scene rather than taking it on trust.
## So what does `rect(1, 1)` return
An ordinary object. Not a string, not an array of numbers — the `Shape` described above:
```ts
rect(1, 1)
segments: [
Write that by hand and you get the same square; `rect` is not needed for it at all.
**THREE segments, not four.** The fourth side is not written: a shape is a closed region, and the
way back to `start` is implied. Adding the fourth is the first thing anybody does, and it is one
segment of zero length.
A circle is the same thing with handles:
```ts
circle(0.5)
segments: [
// ...three more like it
Four cubics, and `0.2761` is not a fudged number but `4/3 · (√2 − 1) · r` — what a handle has to
be for the cubic to lie on the circle. A circle made of straight segments would be a polygon.
Any story will show you this: the **`raw`** switch in the controls makes the Code panel print the
value instead of the call. Nothing on the stage changes — only the answer to "what is it really".
## The builder is not a pose
The five controls in the separate `builder` section — `scaleX`, `scaleY`, `rotate`, `offsetX`,
`offsetY` — are not fields of `Bounded`. They call `transformShape` BEFORE the shape becomes
`bounds`:
```ts
Bounded({
bounds: transformShape(fromSvgPath(d)!, { scaleX: 0.4, scaleY: 0.4, offsetY: -0.2 }),
That is an ordinary kit function, not a catalog mechanism. Move any of the five on a neighbouring
story and the Code panel replaces the bare call with this line. While they sit at identity it is
absent: printing a transform that does nothing would teach a reader to write it.
**What it is for.** A path copied out of Figma, Illustrator or an `.svg` file arrives in its
author's coordinates: hundreds of units instead of fractions, the origin in a corner instead of
the centre, somebody else's scale. The kit does not fit it for you — you fit it, once, and what
travels on is the finished shape.
**When it is not needed: almost always.** `rect`, `circle`, `star` and the rest build a shape
around the origin at the size asked for. There is nothing to fit.
**And what it is NOT.**
| | builder | `Transformable` |
| what it is | preparing a VALUE | a node's pose |
| when it runs | once, when the shape is made | every frame, when it is drawn |
| what the spec carries | coordinates already transformed | `at`, `angle`, `scale` as fields |
| can it be animated | no, it is data by then | yes, that is what it is for |
| is it inherited | there is nothing to inherit | `angle` adds up, `scale` multiplies |
One example makes the difference audible. A rotation in the builder is a shape that IS that way:
a crooked card, drawn crooked. A rotation in `Transformable` is a shape that WAS TURNED: an
ordinary card lying askew. A command to straighten everything to zero reaches the second and
leaves the first alone — rightly, because it straightens poses, not drawings.
Hence the two sections in the panel. `rotate` sat among the `bounds` fields once, and the section
heading then read as "these are the parts of the field" — that `Bounded` has a rotation. It has
none.
## Notes
- Sizes are in units, not pixels. The host is the only part that knows what a unit is worth
on screen, so the same node is the same size on every device.
- `Bounded` draws nothing — no fill, no border, no radius. Appearance comes from `Surfaced`
and the surface it names.
- A curve is flattened to points ONCE, at the edge where something is drawn. Everything below
the model is handed points and has nothing to branch on, which is what lets a debug layer, a
dash walk and a second renderer be written without any of them learning what an ellipse is.
- NOT a collider. A hit test that has to bounce a puck wants an analytic circle, not points,
and it will get one from its own atom — the way Godot, Unity and Box2D all separate the drawn
shape from the colliding one. That is also how an irregular texture carries a perfectly round
collider, which is the whole trick of an air-hockey table.
- `footprint()` returns `undefined` for a node without `Bounded`. That is different from a
box of size zero: one has no area, the other has an area of nothing.
## The shelf below
Every story here has the SAME controls, because there is one field and one way to edit it.
What differs is where each one starts. The panel offers a PRESET — which helper builds the
shape — and that preset's parameters; the Code panel shows the call it makes.

bounds: {
segments: [
This is a `Shape`, and it is what EVERY call on the neighbouring pages turns into. `rect(1, 1)`
returns an object like this one; `star(5, 1, 0.42)` returns the same thing, longer. Both are
written out further down this page.
The arrow is chosen because the kit has no helper for one. A square here would invite "so why not
`rect(1, 1)`" — and lead away from the point, which is that a square IS this.
Three segments for a four-sided outline: the way back to `start` is implied, because a shape is a
closed region. A fourth segment written by hand is a segment of zero length.
ONE control for the whole shape — `bounds` itself, as an object. Cutting it into a `start`
box and a `segments` box would be two controls for one field, which is exactly the lie the
deleted `size`/`bounds` pair told. Add a pair to `segments` and the outline grows a side;
give an entry a `c1` and a `c2` and that side bends.
There is no builder here, and this is the only such page on the shelf: a preset, a width and a
radius here would be precisely what it exists without. Edit the points in the source — the Code
panel shows the whole of it.
docs.bounded.square: The plainest box there is, and the atom's own default: a 1×1 rect.
The outline is TOOLING, not the box. Switch it off in the toolbar and the stage is empty
however large the numbers say the box is — a box is a place taken, not a look.
A square by default has to be said out loud rather than left to be inferred. Read as a claim
about cards it would say "elements are square", which is not what it means: it is the
plainest shape that shows a box exists.
docs.bounded.rectangle: The same sort, different numbers — 1 by 1.4, the proportions of a playing card.
`w` and `h` are the whole of a rect. Units, not pixels: the host decides what a unit is worth
on screen, so this card is the same card on a phone and on a desk monitor.
docs.bounded.line: A run between two places — and the bend is part of the BOX.
`from` and `to` are the ends; `bend` pulls the middle sideways and holds them where they are. At
zero it is a straight line, and that is not a second sort of shape: a curve is where a path's
places are, and `bend` puts one between the ends. `line({ … })` is what the snippet says, and it
is a kit function, not a helper of this website.
The shape is walked out and back, so it encloses nothing and has no inside at all. That costs it
nothing here — `Bounded` paints no pixel either way, and the outline above is the debug layer
showing you the box. What a surface does with a shape like this is `Surfaced → Path`; what stands
docs.bounded.point: A point — a path of one point and no segments at all:
Bounded({ bounds: { start: { x: 0, y: 0 }, segments: [] } })
You should see NOTHING, with the outline switched on. That is the scene. Open the tree below: the
node is there, and its box is zero. This is not the same answer as a node with no `Bounded` at
all: one takes up no room, the other is not in the layout to be asked. `footprint()` tells them
It is needed because games are full of them: the anchor a card flies to, a marker a layout still
has to place, the origin of something that has not arrived yet. A place with no area.
A zero region CONTAINS nothing — but it is somewhere, and everything else can reach it. "Did the
card cover the anchor" is a question about the card's area and the point's coordinate, and it is
answered perfectly well; so is a circle that covered it. What a point cannot be is the one asked
"is this inside you": there is no inside.
So the tolerance for "touched" comes from the ASKER, never from here. A finger is wide, a cursor
is not. Widening the point instead would mean the marker differs depending on who is looking at
it — the mistake of the deleted `size`/`bounds` pair.
docs.bounded.circle: One number, `r`. A circle has nothing else to say.
Inside it is four cubics and nothing more. It becomes a polygon only at the renderer:
`outlineOf` flattens the curves to straight runs against a tolerance measured in units, and for
`r: 0.8` that comes out at 64 points. It happens below the model — what you set here is a
circle, and the tree below reports a circle.
The tolerance is in units rather than pixels, so a small chip and a large one get the same
number of points. The number is chosen so the error is not resolvable by eye at the sizes a
docs.bounded.oval: An ellipse — `ellipse(1.2, 0.8)` — and four cubics is exactly what one is.
A circle is this with equal radii. Not a scaled circle, not a sort of its own: `circle(r)` is
one line that calls `ellipse(r, r)`. Saying it the other way round is what put a tag in the
model for a shape that was one argument away from its neighbour.
A curve stays a curve at any size: what travels is a handful of handles, and flattening happens
once, at the renderer, for the size actually being drawn. Points computed in advance would be
somebody's frozen sampling — an ellipse right up until somebody zoomed in.
docs.bounded.pentagon: `polygon(5, 0.9)` — N corners on a circle, the first one at the top.
The same helper draws a triangle, an octagon and a sixteen-sided coin. Nothing about it is a
special case: it returns a path of straight runs, exactly like the one you would paste.
docs.bounded.star: `star(5, 1, 0.42)` — five points on the outer circle, the notches between them on the inner.
A polygon whose corners alternate between two radii, which is why it needs no new sort.
The kit does not know the word "star"; one helper does, and it is the only place that has to.
Bring the inner radius up towards the outer and it becomes a cog; take it down and the points
turn to spikes. That is what the model would have had to enumerate if shapes were sorts.
docs.bounded.swoosh: The real Nike mark, pasted **as it sits in the file**: `viewBox="135.5 361.38 1000 356.39"`,
coordinates from 135 to 1135, the origin somewhere off to the upper left. Sixteen segments,
Named for the shape, not for the company whose mark it resembles.
## The one story that needs the builder
The kit does not guess what size this was meant to be, and should not. You fit it — once, when
scaleX: 0.0028, scaleY: 0.0028,      // 1000 tool units → 2.8 of ours
offsetX: -1.7794, offsetY: -1.5108,  // the centre of the box onto the origin
The numbers are not eyeballed: the scale is `2.8 / 1000`, and the offset is the centre of the
extent carried to the origin, because `(0,0)` is what a shape is placed and turned by. Out comes
`2.799 × 0.997` units — a shape in units like every other on the shelf.
What travels in the spec is the transformed coordinates. None of this arithmetic survives into
the model, and the builder is not a pose — there is a section about that on the page above.
As a polygon this was a bent banana, and no number of points would have fixed it honestly: a
curve drawn with straight runs is faceted exactly where it turns most, which is exactly where the
eye is looking. Paste your own `d` over it and fit it with the same five numbers.
docs.bounded.pawn: A flared base, a waist, a collar and a ball — the parts a pawn is actually made of, each one a
curve. Straight only where a pawn is straight: the foot it stands on.
This is the point the shelf climbs towards. A piece's box does not have to be the square it
stands on — it can be the piece, and at the size a piece is drawn nobody can tell this outline
Also the honest limit. One shape answers all three questions today — layout, hit, silhouette —
so a silhouette this tight is a hit area this tight: accurate, and harder to tap. The pair of
shapes that would let those answers differ is exactly what was taken out of this atom, and it
returns with the asker that needs it.
